'''Anne Ephrussi''' (born 15 September 1955 in [[Paris]], [[France]]) is a French developmental and molecular [[biologist]]. Her research is focused on the study of [[post-transcriptional regulation]]s such as [[Messenger RNA|mRNA]] localization and translation control in [[molecular biology]] as well as the establishment of polarity axes in cell and developmental biology.<ref name="ephrussi_group">{{cite web |title=Ephrussi Group – RNA localisation and localised translation in development |url=https://www.embl.de/research/units/dev_biology/ephrussi/index.html |access-date=7 September 2022}}</ref> She is director of the EMBL International Centre for Advanced Training (EICAT) program at the [[European Molecular Biology Laboratory]] (EMBL) <ref name="ephrussi_embl">{{cite web |title=Anne Ephrussi, Director of EICAT {{!}} People {{!}} EMBL |url=https://www.embl.org/people/person/413360ff0fd9a8e3bdbdde62fa4ef6415e5c575f3d0638b0d380aefb7d49fc0e/ |website=embl.org |access-date=7 September 2022 |language=en}}</ref><ref name="eicat">{{cite web |title=EICAT |url=https://www.embl.org/training/eicat/ |website=embl.org |access-date=7 September 2022 |language=en}}</ref> since 2005 and served as head of the Developmental Biology Unit from 2007 to 2021.

== Biography ==
Anne Ephrussi studied biology at [[Harvard University]] in the Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology from where she graduated in 1979. She continued to do her [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) in the group of [[Susumu Tonegawa]] where she received her doctoral degree in 1985. Ephrussi performed postdoctoral research at [[Harvard University]] in the lab of [[Tom Maniatis|Thomas Maniatis]] from 1986 to 1989 and at the [[Whitehead Institute|Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research]] with [[Ruth Lehmann]] from 1989 to 1992. Since 1992, Anne Ephrussi has been a group leader at the [[European Molecular Biology Laboratory]] (EMBL). She became the head of EMBL International Centre for Advanced Training in 2005.<ref name="ephrussi_embl" /><ref>[https://www.embl.fr/aboutus/communication_outreach/publications/newsletter/issues/issue40.pdf EMBL Communications – Communicating EMBL’s innovative research programmes and cutting-edge science]</ref> She served as Associate Dean (1999 - 2005) and Dean (2005 - 2008) of Graduate Studies of the [https://www.embl.de/training/eipp/index.html EMBL International PhD program] and as head of the developmental biology unit (2007-2021). She is part of numerous international Scientific Advisory Boards and Panels, organizes international conferences and scientific meetings and evaluates research grant and fellowship applications for a variety of renowned [[funding bodies]].

== Personal Details ==
Anne Ephrussi has French and American citizenship. She is the daughter of [[Boris Ephrussi]] and [[Harriett Ephrussi-Taylor]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Boris Ephrussi (1901-1979) {{!}} The Embryo Project Encyclopedia |url=https://embryo.asu.edu/pages/boris-ephrussi-1901-1979 |website=embryo.asu.edu |access-date=7 September 2022 |language=en}}</ref> She lives in [[Heidelberg]], is married and has one child.

== Research ==
With her research, Anne Ephrussi has contributed to the elucidation of the crucial role that spatial and temporal control of [[Messenger RNA|mRNA]] localization and translation play in [[oocyte]] development and [[cell polarity]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Besse|first1=Florence|last2=Ephrussi|first2=Anne|date=2008|title=Translational control of localized mRNAs: restricting protein synthesis in space and time|journal=Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology|language=en|volume=9|issue=12|pages=971–980|doi=10.1038/nrm2548|pmid=19023284|s2cid=35745917|issn=1471-0072}}</ref>

Ephrussi established that [[oskar (gene)|oskar]] RNA is accumulated at and thereby defines the [[Posterior (anatomy)|posterior]] pole of the ''[[Drosophila]]'' [[oocyte]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ephrussi|first1=Anne|last2=Dickinson|first2=Laura K.|last3=Lehmann|first3=Ruth|date=1991|title=oskar organizes the germ plasm and directs localization of the posterior determinant nanos|journal=Cell|language=en|volume=66|issue=1|pages=37–50|doi=10.1016/0092-8674(91)90137-N|pmid=2070417|s2cid=23006074}}</ref> Aberrant localization and [[Translation (biology)|translation]] leads to germ cell formation defects and mispatterning during development.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ephrussi|first1=Anne|last2=Lehmann|first2=Ruth|date=1992|title=Induction of germ cell formation by oskar|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=358|issue=6385|pages=387–392|doi=10.1038/358387a0|pmid=1641021|issn=0028-0836|bibcode=1992Natur.358..387E|s2cid=4269753}}</ref> Proper localization of [[oskar (gene)|oskar]] mRNA is ensured by concerted actions of the [[exon junction complex]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Markussen|first1=F. H.|last2=Michon|first2=A. M.|last3=Breitwieser|first3=W.|last4=Ephrussi|first4=A.|date=1995|title=Translational control of oskar generates short OSK, the isoform that induces pole plasma assembly|journal=Development|volume=121|issue=11|pages=3723–3732|doi=10.1242/dev.121.11.3723 |issn=0950-1991|pmid=8582284}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Hachet|first1=Olivier|last2=Ephrussi|first2=Anne|date=2004|title=Splicing of oskar RNA in the nucleus is coupled to its cytoplasmic localization|journal=Nature|language=en|volume=428|issue=6986|pages=959–963|doi=10.1038/nature02521|pmid=15118729|issn=0028-0836|bibcode=2004Natur.428..959H|s2cid=4413199}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Ghosh|first1=Sanjay|last2=Marchand|first2=Virginie|last3=Gáspár|first3=Imre|last4=Ephrussi|first4=Anne|date=2012|title=Control of RNP motility and localization by a splicing-dependent structure in oskar mRNA|journal=Nature Structural & Molecular Biology|language=en|volume=19|issue=4|pages=441–449|doi=10.1038/nsmb.2257|pmid=22426546|s2cid=20099525|issn=1545-9993}}</ref> and oskar's [[Three prime untranslated region|3’ UTR]]<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Jambor|first1=Helena|last2=Mueller|first2=Sandra|last3=Bullock|first3=Simon L.|last4=Ephrussi|first4=Anne|date=2014|title=A stem-loop structure directs oskar mRNA to microtubule minus ends|journal=RNA |volume=20|issue=4|pages=429–439|doi=10.1261/rna.041566.113|issn=1469-9001|pmc=3964905|pmid=24572808}}</ref> followed by a [[microtubule]]-based movement. During transport, translation of oskar is repressed by the [[RNA-binding protein]] Bruno, which is in turn released by the binding of activators (e.g. Orb) upon arrival at the posterior pole.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Chekulaeva|first1=Marina|last2=Hentze|first2=Matthias W.|last3=Ephrussi|first3=Anne|date=2006|title=Bruno Acts as a Dual Repressor of oskar Translation, Promoting mRNA Oligomerization and Formation of Silencing Particles|journal=Cell|language=en|volume=124|issue=3|pages=521–533|doi=10.1016/j.cell.2006.01.031|pmid=16469699|s2cid=6308889|doi-access=free}}</ref> After proper localization, oskar RNA is translated and organizes [[germ plasm]] by recruiting other proteins such as Vasa.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Breitwieser|first1=W|last2=Markussen|first2=F H|last3=Horstmann|first3=H|last4=Ephrussi|first4=A|date=1996|title=Oskar protein interaction with Vasa represents an essential step in polar granule assembly.|journal=Genes & Development|language=en|volume=10|issue=17|pages=2179–2188|doi=10.1101/gad.10.17.2179|pmid=8804312|issn=0890-9369|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Her lab's current research continues to focus on spatial and temporal control of translation and which role [[ribonucleoprotein]] complexes ([[Ribonucleoprotein|RNPs]]), [[Cytoskeleton|cytoskeletal]] polarization and [[Motor protein|cytoskeletal motors]] play in RNA localization. Further, the roles of non-canonical [[RNA-binding protein|RNA binding proteins]] in development as well as germ plasm assembly and function are investigated. These questions are tackled using a combination of [[genetics]], [[biochemistry]] and a broad spectrum of [[Cell biology|cell bio]]<nowiki/>logical and imaging approaches using the large ''[[Drosophila melanogaster]]'' oocyte as a model.
